In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Commentary on Surat an-Nazi'at (The Ones Who Pull Out)

It is Meccan, and Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By those who pull out violently﴾. Regarding this there are several opinions. The most apparent of them is that they are the angels who pull out the souls of the disbelievers with severity. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and a group, and something similar is related from Ibn Mas'ud through the narration of Masruq.

His saying: ﴿violently﴾ means with excess, i.e., "they exceed in pulling out" (aghraqa fi al-naz'), meaning they reach the utmost limit.

It is related from al-Hasan that they are the stars which move from horizon to horizon, i.e., they rise and set. And it is related from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that they are the bows, from the expression "pulling the bow" (nazi'at al-qaws) and the drawing of it to its full extent (al-ighraq fihi).

And His saying: ﴿By those that draw out with ease﴾. According to the first view, they are also the angels, who draw out the souls of the disbelievers, meaning they pull them out swiftly. The poet said:

(My worries have become such that they drag out the drags... Syria with me at times and at times in the middle)

In the language, *nashṭ* means pulling. It is said: the soul of the disbeliever is pulled out just as a wet skewer is pulled out of wool. It was also said: the meaning of *al-nāshiṭāt* is that the angels take the souls of the believers with ease, just as a camel is released from its tether.

In the reports: the angels take the soul of the disbeliever with the utmost violence, and when it reaches his collarbone, they return the soul into his body, then pull it out again in this manner several times as a punishment for him. And they take the soul of the believer swiftly and easily.

The second view: the *nāshiṭāt* are the stars, as we have mentioned from al-Ḥasan, and the meaning is the swiftness of their movement. It is said: their return from the west to their risings, and this is for the seven wandering planets. This is in the sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I swear by the retrograding, running, setting ones﴾, as we will explain, as reported by al-Naqqāsh.

The third view: they are the snares (*awhāq*).

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By those who glide along swiftly﴾. According to the first opinion, they are the angels, and their "sabh" (gliding) is their movement between the heavens and the earth. According to the second opinion, they are the stars, and their sabh is their moving within the orbit (falak). The third opinion is that they are the horses, and their sabh is the swiftness of their running; a noble horse is called sābiḥ (swift-gliding).

Regarding His words, ﴿Then those that outstrip, outstripping﴾: according to the first view, they are the angels, and their outstripping is their hastening to righteous deeds and good works.

It is also said: their outstripping is the racing to convey the revelation before the devils eavesdrop on it. According to the second view, they are the stars, one of which outpaces another in its course. According to the third view, they are the horses, likewise one of which outpaces another in a race. And it is said that they are the souls that rush out at the time of death.

al-Suddi also mentioned that the meaning of ﴿Those who drag forth﴾ is the souls and spirits that are drawn out at the time of death.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 5:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then those who arrange (al-mudabbirat) an affair﴾ refer, according to all scholars, to the angels, except for what is reported in a rare narration through the transmission of Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that they are the stars.

The meaning of "arranging" (al-tadbir) on the part of the angels is that God has entrusted to them some of the affairs.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit said: To Jibril are entrusted the armies; to Mikail the rain and the plants; to 'Azra'il the taking of souls; and to Israfil the sending down [of commands]. The affairs are entrusted to them in these matters, [to] the angels. As for when we take it to mean the stars, it is permissible that God, Exalted, attaches to their risings, their settings and their courses various matters, and He attributes the arranging to them in a figurative sense (majaz).

Scholars differed concerning what is sworn by and what the oath is about. As for the first view, which is the more correct of the two: He swore by these things, and God may swear by whatever He wills of His creation. The second view is that its meaning is "and by the Lord of the ones who pull out," so the word "Lord" is implied in these expressions, and He swore by Himself, not by these things.

As for what the oath is about, there are two views. The first is that it is omitted, and the meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected and surely be called to account," and what is similar to that.

The second view is that what the oath is about is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾.

Almighty's saying: ﴿On the Day when the quaking one quakes﴾. Al-rajf (the trembling) and al-rajifa (the quaking one) are agitation and a severe earthquake, and it is in the sense of His saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) shaking﴾. It is also said: al-rajifa is the first Blast (al-sayha al-ula) by which He causes all creatures to die.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 7:

And His saying: ﴿Followed by the Radifah (the second blast)﴾ has two opinions. One of them: it is the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah). The other: it is the second blast (al-Sayhah al-Thaniyah).

And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that between them is forty years, and the sky rains during these forty years, so the earth stirs, and people sprout in their graves, then their spirits are returned to them at the second blast.
Also the Most High's saying: ﴿Hearts that Day will be trembling﴾, i.e., agitated. It is said: wajafa yajifu and wajaba yajibu, with the same meaning. It is also said: wajifah, i.e., fearful.
"And His words: ﴿Their eyes cast down, humbled﴾ meaning: abased."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 10:

And His saying: ﴿They say﴾ — this is a report of their statement in the world, meaning: they say in the world: "Shall we indeed be returned to the first state?" (al-hafirah), that is, to our original condition. The meaning is: Shall we be returned alive after we have died? This is said in denial. It is said: "He returned on his hafirah" (heel-track, i.e., by the same path) when he went back the way he came.

The Arabs say: "The haggling is at the hafirah," meaning: at the first word, that is, at the beginning of the bargaining.

And the poet said:

(Hafirah upon baldness and gray hair... God forbid, from foolishness and shame.)

And al-Suddi said: ﴿Shall we indeed be returned to the hafirah?﴾ means: to life. This is in accordance with what we have said. It was also said: to the Fire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 11:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Are we, when we are bones, decayed?﴾ It is also read as "nākhirah" (ناخرة). Al-Farrā' said: the two are one and the same, and they mean that which is worn out and perishing.

It is related from Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā' that al-nakhirah is that which has decayed, while al-nākhirah is that which has not yet decayed. It is related from Wakī' that he said: it is that into which the wind enters so that it hollows out (tankhur), and this is also transmitted from the people of lexicography (ahl al-lughah).

They said, "That would then be a losing return."

That is, a return entailing loss. The meaning is: we would be in loss if we were returned. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is that they would suffer loss when they return.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "Khasirah" means "false," that is, "it will not come to pass."
And His saying: ﴿It will be but a single shout﴾ is an informing about the ease of the matter for God, in bringing it about. The zajrah (a single cry, shout) is the ṣayḥah (cry, blast).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 14:

And His saying: ﴿Then they will be at the surface of the earth.﴾ The well-known view is that al-Sahirah is the surface of the earth, meaning that they will come out from its belly to its back. The earth was called al-sahirah (the wakeful) because on it is the wakefulness (sahr) and sleep of creation.

Al-Nakha'i said: "﴿Then they will be at the surface of the earth﴾" means: above the earth.

It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: al-Sahirah is a mountain beside Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). The poet said concerning al-sahirah:

(For indeed your grave is the dust of al-sahirah... then you will return after it to al-hafirah.)

(After we were bones, decayed.)
"The Most High's saying: ﴿Has there come to you the story of Moses?﴾ That is: indeed it has come to you."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 16:

And His saying: ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾. That is: the purified (al-muqaddas, i.e. the purified valley).

And His saying: ﴿Tuwa﴾. That is: it was made holy and sanctified twice (tuwiya bi-l-barakah wa-l-taqdis marratayn). It is said: He named it Tuwa because Musa stepped on it with his foot. It is said: it is the name of the valley. It is said: it is the land between Madinah and Egypt.

Al-Hasan recited "Tuwa" with a kasra on the ta' (Ṭiwā). The well-known reading is Tuwa, and it is not declined (ghayr munsarif) because it is the name of a place within the valley and it is a proper noun (ma'rifah). It is related from al-Zajjaj that he said: It is permissible that it be a derived form (ma'dul) from ṭāwin, and for this reason it is not declined, like ʿAmr, which is a derived form (ma'dul) of ʿĀmir. It was also read as declined (maṣrūf), and they recited:

﴿Aʿādhil, inna al-lawma fi ghayr kunhihi ... ʿala ṭawā min ghayyika al-mutaraddid﴾.
The phrase "And [His] saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, indeed he has transgressed﴾" has already been explained, and transgression (al-tughyan) is exceeding the limit.

And His saying: ﴿So say, "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ It is also read "tazakka" with both letters doubled (tashdid).

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: It is not permissible to read it with both doubled; it is permissible with the lighter reading (takhfif), because tazakka means giving zakat.

As for His saying ﴿tazakka﴾, it means entering into the purity of Islam. Abu 'Ubayd followed him in this. [Al-]Nahhas, in his tafsir, mentioned that this is an error: tazakka and tazakka have one meaning; tazakka is the assimilated form (idgham), and tazakka has one letter removed from it. It is said: zakkahu Allah, meaning He purified him through Islam, so he became tazakka. It is also said of one who gives the zakat of his wealth: tazakka.
And His saying: ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him﴾. That is: when you attain guidance, your conduct will become good.
And His saying: ﴿So He showed him the greatest sign﴾. It is said: it is the staff. It is also said: it is the white hand. And it is said: both of them.

Pharaoh's words and deeds, as he is described in the passage, are as follows: "And his saying: ﴿But he denied and disobeyed, then he turned his back, striving﴾" — that is, he turned away and began to strive to nullify the matter of Musa (Moses).

Pharaoh's words and deeds, as he is described in the passage, are as follows: "And his saying: ﴿But he denied and disobeyed, then he turned his back, striving﴾" — that is, he turned away and began to strive to nullify the matter of Musa (Moses).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 23–24:

And His saying: ﴿Then he gathered [his people] and called out﴾. Al-hashr (gathering) is the assembling of [people] from every direction.

And His saying: ﴿and called out﴾, meaning he called out to them and said to them: ﴿"I am your lord, the Most High"﴾, meaning: there is no lord above me.

Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh was a dwarf (ʿilj) from the people of Isfahan, four spans tall (ashbār). It is narrated from Mujahid that he was a dwarf from the people of Hamadhan, and from some others that he was from the people of Istakhr.

It is mentioned in the narrative that Musa said to Pharaoh: "For you is a kingdom that does not pass away, and a youth in which there is no old age, and for you is Paradise in the Hereafter, so say: 'He is my Lord and I am His servant.'" Pharaoh said: "Until I consult Haman." When he consulted him, [Haman] said: "Will you become a servant after having been worshipped? Do not say this."

So he refused to say it.

Al-Naqqash mentioned this in his tafsir.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 23–24:

And His saying: ﴿Then he gathered [his people] and called out﴾. Al-hashr (gathering) is the assembling of [people] from every direction.

And His saying: ﴿and called out﴾, meaning he called out to them and said to them: ﴿"I am your lord, the Most High"﴾, meaning: there is no lord above me.

Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh was a dwarf (ʿilj) from the people of Isfahan, four spans tall (ashbār). It is narrated from Mujahid that he was a dwarf from the people of Hamadhan, and from some others that he was from the people of Istakhr.

It is mentioned in the narrative that Musa said to Pharaoh: "For you is a kingdom that does not pass away, and a youth in which there is no old age, and for you is Paradise in the Hereafter, so say: 'He is my Lord and I am His servant.'" Pharaoh said: "Until I consult Haman." When he consulted him, [Haman] said: "Will you become a servant after having been worshipped? Do not say this."

So he refused to say it.

Al-Naqqash mentioned this in his tafsir.

Wa-qawluhu: ﴿Fa-akhadhahu Allah nakal al-akhirah wa-al-ula﴾ — that is: Allah seized him with a seizure as an exemplary punishment (nakal) for his two sayings, the last and the first. His first saying was His words: ﴿I know of no god for you other than Me﴾, and his last saying was His words: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾. It is also said: he was made an example of and punished in this world and the Hereafter. In this world it was drowning, and in the Hereafter it is the Fire.
In that is indeed a lesson for whoever fears (Allah), meaning: a warning and reflection for whoever fears Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 27:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is it the heaven? He built it.﴾ He argues against them with these verses concerning His power over the resurrection. The meaning is: is your re-creation as a new creation more difficult, or the creation of the heaven? This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Or the heaven, He built it﴾, its meaning is: or the heaven which He built? It was also said that the meaning is: are you more difficult in creation, or the heaven? Then the speech is complete, and He said: ﴿He built it﴾, that is, Allah, may He be exalted, built it.

The verse is ﴿رفع سمكها فسواها﴾, "He raised its canopy and made it even." Translation of the commentary:

And His saying, ﴿He raised its canopy and made it even﴾, is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do you see any fissure?﴾ That is, any cracks or openings. It has also been said that the meaning of leveling (taswiyah) here is that some parts of it are not higher than others, nor lower than others. And al-samk (the canopy) means elevation.

And His saying: ﴿And He darkened its night and brought forth its daylight﴾, meaning: He made its night dark.

And His saying: ﴿and brought forth its daylight﴾, meaning: He made its day manifest. It was also said: He made its light appear. He attributed the darkness and the light to the sky (al-sama'), because they appear from the direction of the sky at the rising and setting of the sun.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 30:

﴿And the earth after that He spread out.﴾ That is: He expanded it.

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

(And He scattered creation upon it when He spread it out... they are its dwellers until the Calling-out [Day of Resurrection])

And Sa'id ibn Zayd said:

(I have submitted my face to the One to whom I have submitted... to whom the earth bears heavy rocks)

He spread it out, then when it was made level He fixed it firmly, and set upon it mountains.

As for His saying ﴿after that﴾, it means: along with that. It is also said: He created the earth before the heaven, as He said in "Ha Mim, the Prostration" [surah 41], and then He spread it out after the creation of the heaven.

And in a report from Ibn 'Abbas: there was nothing but the Throne and the water. He created upon the water a rock like a mortar (fahr), then He created over it a smoke clinging to it, then He created a foam on the water. Then He lifted the smoke from the rock, and created the earth from the rock, the heaven from the smoke, and the mountains from the foam.
And His saying: ﴿He brings forth from it its water and its pasture﴾. That is: He brought forth from the earth the water for the life of souls, and the pasture for the livestock.
"And the mountains—He set them firmly": that is, He fixed them in place.

And His saying, ﴿as a provision for you﴾, meaning: as an enjoyment for you. ﴿And for your cattle﴾. It is in the accusative because its meaning is "for the enjoyment," and then the governing preposition, the لام (lam), was removed, so the noun became accusative (manṣūb).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 34:

The word of the Exalted: ﴿So when the great calamity comes﴾. Al-ṭāmmah (calamity) in the language is the great misfortune. It was also said: it is the matter that cannot be borne and cannot be withstood. It is said: "The valley overflowed (ṭamma) when there came from it what cannot be withstood and it covered everything." It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that al-ṭāmmah is a name of the Resurrection, and the Resurrection was named ṭāmmah because it overwhelms (taṭumm) everything, that is, it rises above everything.

In some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that he said: "There is no calamity except that there is above it a greater calamity." This is a gharīb (strange, weak in chain) report.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿Yawma yatadhakkaru al-insanu ma sa'a﴾ ayy: yadhkur.

His saying: ﴿And Hell is brought forth for whoever sees﴾. In the tafsir (exegesis) it is said: the wisdom in displaying Hell is that the disbelievers witness the place of their punishment, and that the believers may know from what torment they were saved.

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 79, verses 37–38:**

And His saying: ﴿As for he who transgressed and preferred the worldly life﴾, i.e., over the Hereafter.

Abu al-Husayn Ibn Faris related in his tafsir, from Hudhayfah, that whoever eats at a table with three kinds of food has preferred the worldly life. He also cited a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prefers the worldly life over the Hereafter, Allah will scatter his concerns, and then He will not care which of them destroys him."
And His saying: ﴿Then indeed, Hellfire will be the refuge﴾ — meaning, his refuge is the Hellfire, and it is the greatest part of the Fire.

And His saying: ﴿But as for one who feared the standing before his Lord﴾, i.e., his standing before his Lord for the reckoning.

And His saying: ﴿and restrained the soul from desire﴾, i.e., from what it desires and craves contrary to the Sharia (divine law).

And as for the one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from its desire, then indeed Paradise is his refuge. That is: his station and place of return is Paradise.

Some of the exegetes mention that the first verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, 'Uqbah and 'Utbah, the two sons of Abu Lahab, and a group [of others], and the second verse was revealed concerning Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr. He had shielded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with his own self on the Day of Uhud, until the arrowheads entered into his body, and he was martyred on that day. He was the bearer of the banner of the Muhajirun.

Divine saying, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it take place?﴾ That is: when is its establishment? "Mursaha" means its termination (muntaha), and the meaning is about its reality (ma'hiyyatuha).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 43:

And His saying: ﴿In what are you concerned with mentioning it?﴾ That is: what is your business with, and what is your knowledge of, the time of the establishment of the Hour? In some tafsirs: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to ask Jibril often when the Hour would be, so when Allah the Exalted revealed this verse, he refrained, withheld himself, and did not ask after that." And it is like the saying of one person to another: "What is your business with this matter?" And in it is a rebuke for him against asking.

Translation:

His saying: ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, meaning: the ultimate knowledge of its establishment (belongs to Him). It was also said that its meaning is: whoever is asked about it says, "God knows best," so its knowledge is referred back to God.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 46:

And His saying: ﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾, meaning: the first part of a day or the last part of a day. The first part of the day is from the rising of the sun until it rises high, and the last part of the day is from the afternoon (al-'asr) until its setting. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they had not remained but an hour of a day, a message delivered﴾. If it is said: how does he attribute the morning of the day (duha al-nahar) to its evening, when the morning of the day is only attributed to the day? In what way is this attribution correct? The answer: such a construction is permissible in the speech of the Arabs, and they do this, intending by such an attribution the attribution to the day.

The poet said:

("We attacked 'Amir in her abode, the living of the crescent or its nights.")

It has also been said that the meaning of that is: ﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾, that is: a day among the days. So what is meant by the evening is the day, and the morning is also the day. If it is said: how is this assumption valid, when you hold that they are punished in their graves? The answer: they will fall into a faint between the two blows of the Trumpet, and when they are resurrected they will think of what is between them as [brief], because they forgot the punishment during that faint. And God knows best.
